candidates.quote: Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one.
candidates.author: Plato
candidates.locator: 279b to 279c, the closing prayer of Socrates
candidates.speaker: Socrates
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is a prayer for inward beauty rather than for anything to happen, which is the only thing a quiet morning can actually be asked for.

candidates.quote: You stir man to take pleasure in praising you, because you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
candidates.author: Augustine of Hippo
candidates.locator: Book I, ch. 1 (I.i.1), the opening paragraph
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names the restlessness a person wakes with and calls rest the point of it, which is the month in one sentence.

candidates.quote: What a strange, demented feeling it gives me when I realize I have spent whole days before this inkstone, with nothing better to do, jotting down at random whatever nonsensical thoughts have entered my head.
candidates.author: Yoshida Kenko
candidates.whyThisMonth: A whole book of quiet attention opens by admitting that an idle hour at the desk feels like nothing at all: permission for the empty room.

candidates.quote: We must reserve a back shop all our own, entirely free, in which to establish our real liberty and our principal retreat and solitude.
candidates.author: Michel de Montaigne
candidates.whyThisMonth: The back shop is a room you can keep even in a full house, and at six in the morning it is the one you are standing in.

candidates.quote: I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
candidates.author: Blaise Pascal
candidates.locator: section II, no. 139 (Brunschvicg), in The Harvard Classics vol. 48, 1910
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous diagnosis of restlessness in European philosophy, and the cure it implies takes no equipment: stay in the room.

candidates.quote: Noise is the most impertinent of all forms of interruption. It is not only an interruption, but also a disruption of thought.
candidates.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
candidates.locator: ‘On Noise’, in Studies in Pessimism: A Series of Essays (Swan Sonnenschein, 1890)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It takes the side of the reader who wants quiet and gives the wish a reason: thought needs silence the way a plant needs light.

candidates.quote: Every one knows what attention is. It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought.
candidates.author: William James
candidates.locator: vol. I, ch. XI, ‘Attention’, pp. 403 to 404 (Henry Holt, 1890)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The definition the whole month rests on: attention is a taking possession, something you do, not something that happens to you.

candidates.quote: For all the toll the desert takes of a man it gives compensations, deep breaths, deep sleep, and the communion of the stars.
candidates.author: Mary Austin
candidates.locator: ch. 1, ‘The Land of Little Rain’, near the end of the chapter (Houghton Mifflin, 1903)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It counts what an empty place gives back, and the list is short, physical and available before sunrise.

candidates.quote: Mysticism is the art of union with Reality.
candidates.author: Evelyn Underhill
candidates.locator: ch. I, ‘What is Mysticism?’, the definition about a third of the way in
candidates.whyThisMonth: It makes contemplation an art, something practised badly at first and then better, rather than a mood that visits the lucky.

candidates.quote: If I were asked to name the chief benefit of the house, I should say: the house shelters day-dreaming, the house protects the dreamer, the house allows one to dream in peace.
candidates.author: Gaston Bachelard
candidates.locator: ch. 1, ‘The House. From Cellar to Garret’ (Orion Press, 1964)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Read in the room it describes, it turns an ordinary house at first light into the thing that is doing the sheltering.

candidates.quote: Leisure is a form of silence, of that silence which is the prerequisite of the apprehension of reality: only the silent hear and those who do not remain silent do not hear.
candidates.author: Josef Pieper
candidates.locator: the title essay, ‘Leisure, the Basis of Culture’ (Faber and Faber, 1952)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It argues that an unearned quiet hour is not laziness but the condition for hearing anything at all, which defends the morning to anyone who begrudges it.

candidates.quote: While washing the dishes one should only be washing the dishes, which means that while washing the dishes one should be completely aware of the fact that one is washing the dishes.
candidates.author: Thich Nhat Hanh
candidates.locator: the section ‘Washing the dishes to wash the dishes’ (Beacon Press, 1976)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It puts the month inside the first dull chore of the day, which is where a reader at six can actually try it.

candidates.quote: Silence remains, inescapably, a form of speech (in many instances, of complaint or indictment) and an element in a dialogue.
candidates.author: Susan Sontag
candidates.locator: ‘The Aesthetics of Silence’, the opening essay (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969); first printed in Aspen no. 5 and 6, 1967
candidates.whyThisMonth: It keeps the month honest: silence is never merely absence, and the reader is asked what theirs is saying.

candidates.quote: Lying is done with words, and also with silence.
candidates.author: Adrienne Rich
candidates.work: On Lies, Secrets, and Silence: Selected Prose 1966 to 1978
candidates.locator: ‘Women and Honor: Some Notes on Lying’ (1975), in the 1979 W. W. Norton collection
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month praises silence, and this is the sentence that tells the reader which of their silences is not worth keeping.

candidates.author: May Sarton
candidates.locator: the entry of September 15th, 1970, the opening sentences (W. W. Norton, 1973)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Four words that ask for nothing except that the reader start where they are, in the weather they actually have.

candidates.quote: There is a really deep well inside me. And in it dwells God. Sometimes I am there, too.
candidates.author: Etty Hillesum
candidates.work: An Interrupted Life: The Diaries of Etty Hillesum 1941 to 1943
candidates.whyThisMonth: The well is reached by sitting still and not by striving, and the last three words admit how rarely anyone gets there.
